sources.news_title: Former Kansas senator Nancy Kassebaum Baker, who made history in the U.S. Senate, dies at 94
sources.text:
Former Kansas senator Nancy Kassebaum Baker, who made history in the U.S. Senate, dies at 94
Former U.S. Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker, a trailblazer who became the first woman to represent Kansas in the Senate, has died. She was 94.
Her son said she died Friday of natural causes.
Kassebaum Baker, a Republican, won her first Senate race in 1978 with nearly 54% of the vote, defeating Democrat William R. Roy. She was the only woman serving in the Senate at the time and the first elected to the chamber without following a husband into office.
Her support grew during her three terms. She won reelection in 1984 with about 76% of the vote and again in 1990 with nearly 74%. She chose not to seek reelection in 1996 and left office in January 1997 after 18 years in the Senate.
After retiring, Kassebaum Baker remained active in public service through advisory committees and boards.
Kansas leaders remembered her Saturday as a principled and independent voice who put the state first.
“Kansas lost part of its soul when Nancy Kassebaum died,” Gov. Laura Kelly said. “Humble, unassuming, while focused and fearless, Senator Kassebaum lived a life that mattered. I will miss her.”
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran called Kassebaum Baker “a trailblazer who put the well-being of Kansans first.” Moran, who campaigned for her in western Kansas during her first Senate race, said she was never afraid to challenge him but remained a friend and encourager.
“She was deeply respected across our state, and Kansans remain grateful for the way in which she represented us with such intelligence and integrity,” Moran said. “She will be deeply missed, but her legacy will never be forgotten.”
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall also offered condolences to her family.
“She was a true Kansan who dedicated years of her life to serving our state and made history as Kansas’ first woman to serve in the U.S. Senate,” Marshall said. “Laina and I are keeping her family and loved ones in our prayers.”

A woman who made history in the United States Senate has died at the age of 94.
Former Kansas Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker passed away Friday, August 21, according to her family.
The Republican served Kansas for 18 years and built a national reputation as an independent lawmaker who was willing to work across party lines.
But her election meant something even bigger.
Kassebaum Baker was the first woman elected to a full Senate term without having first been appointed to fill a vacancy created by her husband.
She was also the first woman to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate.
WIBW reported that Kassebaum Baker’s family confirmed her death Saturday morning. A private memorial service will be held at a later date, allowing relatives and close friends to honor her away from the public spotlight that followed much of her career.
The family asked those wishing to honor her to consider supporting the Kansas 4-H Foundation or the Capper Foundation in lieu of flowers.
Kassebaum Baker had celebrated her 94th birthday less than a month before her death. She was born in Topeka and spent nearly two decades carrying Kansas’ voice into the nation’s capital.
Her family’s announcement emphasized the support she received from relatives and friends around the world, along with the successes, challenges and deep love for Kansas that marked her life.
Tributes began pouring in from Kansas leaders as news of her death spread.
Sen. Roger Marshall remembered Kassebaum Baker as a devoted Kansan who made history and dedicated her life to serving the state:
Saddened to hear of the passing of Senator Kassebaum.
She was a true Kansan who dedicated years of her life to serving our state and made history as Kansas’ first woman to serve in the U.S. Senate. Laina and I are keeping her family and loved ones in our prayers. pic.twitter.com/MHkAgFGUoY
— Dr. Roger Marshall (@RogerMarshallMD) August 22, 2026
Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson praised her independence and decency, while Rep. Derek Schmidt remembered the former senator as an early mentor who left him with a lifetime of cherished memories.
Drew Altman, president and CEO of the health policy organization KFF, remembered Kassebaum Baker as both an effective public servant and a valued former trustee:
One of the most dedicated, human, effective public servants I have ever known. And a wonderful former KFF trustee. https://t.co/lLAtfya0gU
— Drew Altman (@DrewAltman) August 22, 2026
A Trailblazer Who Won On Her Own
Kassebaum Baker entered the Senate in 1978. She was the chamber’s only woman when she arrived.
The U.S. Senate Historical Office says the number of women serving in the chamber had grown to nine by the time she retired in 1997. Her career therefore spanned a profound institutional change that she helped make possible simply by winning, serving and leading.
She won three statewide elections in Kansas, including overwhelming reelection victories in 1984 and 1990. Those landslides showed that her popularity extended well beyond the Republican voters who first nominated her.
Her rise was especially remarkable because she began the 1978 Republican primary as an underdog in a crowded nine-candidate field.
She went on to win the nomination and then defeated Democrat Bill Roy in the general election, proving that the underdog campaign had become a statewide movement.
Kassebaum Baker came from one of Kansas’ best-known political families. Her father, Alf Landon, served as governor.
Landon also became the Republican presidential nominee who challenged Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1936.
But she built a political identity of her own—pragmatic, understated and fiercely connected to her home state.
During her final term, she became the only woman then leading a Senate committee. Her retirement closed an era in which she had watched the chamber change from one woman to nine.
An Independent Voice In Washington
The U.S. House Office of the Historian records that Kassebaum Baker served from December 1978 until January 1997 and chaired the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources during her final term. She chose not to seek a fourth term and left office after nearly two full decades in Washington.
That made her only the second woman in Senate history to chair a standing committee.
Her work ranged from arms control and the fight against apartheid in South Africa to aviation liability reform and health care. The breadth of that portfolio reflected a senator who moved comfortably between major international questions and practical domestic policy.
She also served as a senior member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, giving her a prominent voice on Cold War policy and America’s role overseas.
One of the most lasting pieces of her legislative legacy came in 1996, when she worked with Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy on the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act.
The law became widely known as HIPAA and remains part of everyday American life three decades later.
Former Tennessee Sen. Lamar Alexander remembered her commitment to education and health care, along with the respect she earned in both Kansas and Tennessee:
As a US Senator from Kansas, Nancy Kassebaum was honest, independent and an avid supporter of improving American schools and health care. Later, as the wife of Tennessee senator Howard Baker Jr., she enriched our state. She was admired wherever she lived. To Nancy’s Kansas and…
— Lamar Alexander (@SenAlexander) August 22, 2026
Her congressional record also included work on budget deficits, general aviation and protections for people trying to keep health coverage when changing jobs.
Kassebaum Baker was a moderate Republican who did not always follow party leadership. Her willingness to take politically difficult positions frustrated conservatives at times, but it also helped her develop a reputation for putting her own judgment ahead of Washington pressure.
A Life Rooted In Kansas
Nancy Landon Kassebaum was born in Topeka on July 29, 1932.
She earned a political science degree from the University of Kansas and a master’s degree in diplomatic history from the University of Michigan.
Before entering the Senate, she worked as a radio station executive, served on a local school board and spent time on the staff of Kansas Sen. James Pearson.
After leaving Washington, she returned to the Kansas Flint Hills and continued taking on public-service roles.
In 1996, she married former Tennessee Sen. Howard Baker, who had served as Senate majority leader, White House chief of staff under President Ronald Reagan and later U.S. ambassador to Japan. He died in 2014.
Kassebaum Baker’s son Bill said his mother loved Kansas, its people and the privilege of representing them.
Her family echoed that same theme in announcing her death: a long life filled with achievement, challenge and a deep devotion to the state she called home.
Nancy Kassebaum Baker leaves behind more than a place in the history books. She leaves the example of a public servant who broke barriers without allowing the barrier itself to define her.
This is a Guest Post from our friends over at WLTReport. View the original article here.

Nancy Kassebaum Baker, former U.S. senator from Kansas, dies at 94
sources.text:
Nancy Kassebaum Baker, former U.S. senator from Kansas, dies at 94
Nancy Kassebaum Baker, a Kansas governor's daughter who became the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without following a spouse into office, has died, her son Bill Kassebaum told CBS News on Saturday. She was 94.
Kassebaum Baker died Friday, he said.
Bill Kassebaum told CBS News that his mother was "an independent voice that was willing to do what was right for Kansas and the country," which he said sometimes meant going against her party.
"She was also willing to talk to her constituents, even when they didn't agree, and openly discuss her votes and stances," he said, adding that while people may not have agreed with her, they appreciated her willingness to talk.
Kassebaum Baker was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1978 and served three terms. Her modest demeanor endeared her to voters of all political stripes, though she shared the moderate, progressive Republican politics of her father, Gov. Alf Landon, the unsuccessful 1936 GOP nominee for president. Even after leaving the Senate early in 1997, she continued taking on public service roles.
She married former Sen. Howard Baker, a Tennessee Republican, in 1996. He died in 2014.
Kassebaum Baker remained an icon for Kansans generally. She could work with Senate colleagues of all political philosophies, and a 1996 health insurance law bore her name, along with that of liberal Massachusetts Sen. Ted Kennedy.
Her election to the Senate brought her immediate national attention. When she announced her retirement, she was among eight women senators and the only one to chair a Senate committee, the Labor and Human Resources panel.
She was also in a dwindling bloc of moderate-to-liberal Republicans, having supported, for example, a ban on assault weapons championed by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
Yet she never polarized Kansas conservatives as other GOP moderates did. She connected with voters because she never seemed caught up in the trappings of power, and when she retired, she acknowledged, "I'd rather cuddle up and do needlepoint all day."
She was born on July 29, 1932, as her father, an oilman from Independence, was running for the first of his two terms as governor. She earned a political science degree from the University of Kansas and a master's degree in diplomatic history from the University of Michigan in the mid-1950s.
She was a radio-station executive, spent a year in the 1970s on the staff of Kansas Sen. James Pearson and served on the school board in the Wichita suburb of Maize. She had four children with her first husband, Phil Kassebaum, including Bill, who served a term in the Kansas House. The marriage ended in divorce in 1979.
When Kassebaum Baker decided to run for the U.S. Senate, she figured that "a woman with a background different from a man might be appealing" to people growing weary of politics. Pundits at the time estimated a Senate race would require the then-huge-for-Kansas sum of $1 million. In the first quarter of 1978, she spent less than $12,000 on her campaign, and saw herself "at the bottom of the totem pole."
However, nine candidates crowded the primary field, including three state senators and a prominent Wichita businessman. Kassebaum Baker won the GOP nomination with less than 31% of the vote.
Running as Nancy Landon Kassebaum, she won almost 54% of the vote that November against former two-term Democratic congressman Bill Roy.
Her moderate politics quickly came to the fore when only months later, she refused to endorse an amendment to the U.S. Constitution to require a balanced budget.
"We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution," she said.
Her father, who would die at age 100 in 1987, still cast a long political shadow during her first years in office. Though he'd overwhelmingly lost the 1936 presidential race to Democratic incumbent Franklin Roosevelt, he later became an elder statesman for the party. A lecture series named for him at Kansas State University attracted presidents and foreign leaders.
Kassebaum Baker became even more popular in her time. She won re-election in 1984 with 76% of the vote and in 1990 with 74% of the vote.
But she frustrated conservative activists, despite her popularity. She said her vote in favor of the assault weapons ban inspired the angriest mail of her career.
She'd contemplated not seeking a third term, but Republican leaders had prevailed upon her to run one more time. In 1996, when she decided not to seek re-election, she said she would return to a ranch and 90-year-old farmhouse in Kansas' scenic Flint Hills and babysit her grandchildren — she had seven, as well as two great-grandchildren.
When there was brief talk of naming a new highway in Topeka after her, she said, "Oh, goodness. Absolutely not — no."
She and Baker kept their romance low-key, and speculation about a possible marriage didn't emerge until mid-1996, in a Washington Post story. They married that December.
It was the first time a man and a woman who had both served in the Senate had wed. Baker was elected to three terms and served from 1967 to 1985 before becoming President Ronald Reagan's chief of staff. His first wife, Joy, had died in 1993 after a long battle with cancer.
After the marriage, public service still beckoned, including as a member of a bipartisan commission on campaign finance reform under Clinton and on a British commission in Africa in 2004-05.
President George W. Bush named her husband ambassador to Japan in 2001, and she went with him for the four-year posting. Baker said she became an important figure in the Asian nation.
Before she left for Tokyo, she told a reporter she saw her stint in Japan as an adventure but added, "All I can say is, I will miss the Kansas prairie."
Later in life, Kassebaum Baker broke with the Republican Party as it became more conservative, endorsing Democratic candidates for Kansas governor and U.S. senator, including Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly both times — even though Kelly's 2022 GOP opponent, then state Attorney General Derek Schmidt, had worked on her Senate staff.
She also declared in 2021 that President Trump should be impeached after Trump supporters attacked the U.S. Capitol, hoping to stop congressional certification of Mr. Trump's defeat in 2020 by Democrat Joe Biden.
"This just has gone too far," she told Kansas City's KMBC.

Nancy Kassebaum Baker, pioneering Kansas senator, dies at 94
Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the former Kansas senator and Republican moderate, has died at 94. Her career broke barriers for women and embodied bipartisan public service.
Nancy Kassebaum Baker, a former US senator from Kansas who became the first woman elected to the Senate without following a spouse into office, has died at the age of 94. She died of natural causes on Friday, according to her son, Bill Kassebaum.
Remembered as a moderate, independent-minded Republican, Kassebaum Baker served three terms in the US Senate after first being elected in 1978. She remained a widely respected figure in Kansas after leaving office in early 1997 and continued to take on public service roles in the years that followed.
"She loved Kansas. She loved people from Kansas and representing Kansas for 18 years in the US Senate," Bill Kassebaum told The Associated Press. "She was an independent-minded Republican who was willing to stand up for what she thought was right, even if that meant going against the party."
Her modest demeanour helped her connect with voters across political lines, even as she shared the moderate and progressive Republican views of her father, former Kansas governor Alf Landon, the party's unsuccessful 1936 presidential nominee. She later married former senator Howard Baker, a Tennessee Republican, in 1996. He died in 2014.
Kassebaum Baker remained an icon in Kansas and was known for working with colleagues across political divisions. A 1996 health insurance law carried her name along with that of liberal Massachusetts senator Ted Kennedy. When she announced her retirement, she was one of eight women in the Senate and the only one chairing a Senate committee, the Labour and Human Resources panel.
She was part of a shrinking group of moderate-to-liberal Republicans and supported, among other measures, an assault weapons ban backed by Democratic President Bill Clinton. Even so, she did not alienate Kansas conservatives in the way some other Republican moderates did. She projected little interest in the trappings of power and, on retiring, said, "I'd rather cuddle up and do needlepoint all day."
Born on July 29, 1932, while her father was campaigning for his first term as governor, she studied political science at the University of Kansas and later earned a master's degree in diplomatic history from the University of Michigan. She worked as a radio-station executive, spent a year in the 1970s on the staff of Kansas senator James Pearson, and served on the school board in the Wichita suburb of Maize. She had four children with her first husband, Phil Kassebaum, including Bill Kassebaum, who later served a term in the Kansas House. Their marriage ended in divorce in 1979.
When she decided to run for the Senate, Kassebaum Baker believed that "a woman with a background different from a man might be appealing" to voters tired of politics. At a time when commentators estimated that a Senate race would need the then-large-for-Kansas sum of USD 1 million, she spent less than USD 12,000 in the first quarter of 1978 and said she saw herself as "at the bottom of the totem pole".
She still emerged from a crowded nine-candidate Republican primary, which included three state senators and a prominent Wichita businessman, winning the nomination with less than 31 per cent of the vote. Running as Nancy Landon Kassebaum, she went on to defeat former two-term Democratic congressman Bill Roy with almost 54 per cent of the vote in the general election.
Her moderate politics became clear early in her Senate career when, only months later, she refused to back an amendment to the US Constitution requiring a balanced budget. "We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution," she said. During her early years in office, her father continued to cast a long political shadow. Though he had lost heavily to Franklin Roosevelt in 1936, he later became an elder statesman in the Republican Party, and a lecture series named after him at Kansas State University drew presidents and foreign leaders.
Kassebaum Baker's own popularity grew further over time. She was re-elected in 1984 with 76 per cent of the vote and again in 1990 with 74 per cent. But she often frustrated conservative activists despite her appeal with voters, and she said her vote for the assault weapons ban brought the angriest mail of her career.
She had considered not seeking a third term, but Republican leaders persuaded her to run again. When she chose not to seek re-election in 1996, she said she would return to a ranch and a 90-year-old farmhouse in Kansas' Flint Hills and babysit her grandchildren. She had seven grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. When there was brief talk of naming a new highway in Topeka after her, she responded, "Oh, goodness. Absolutely not - no."
Her relationship with Howard Baker was kept largely private, and talk of a possible marriage surfaced only in mid-1996 in a Washington Post report. They married in December that year, becoming the first man and woman who had both served in the Senate to wed. Howard Baker had served three terms from 1967 to 1985 and later became President Ronald Reagan's chief of staff. His first wife, Joy, had died in 1993 after a long battle with cancer.
After their marriage, Kassebaum Baker continued in public life, including service on a bipartisan commission on campaign finance reform under Clinton and on a British commission in Africa in 2004-05. When President George W. Bush appointed Howard Baker ambassador to Japan in 2001, she joined him for the four-year posting and became an important public figure there. Before leaving for Tokyo, she told a reporter, "All I can say is, I will miss the Kansas prairie."
In later years, she broke with the Republican Party as it moved further to the right, backing Democratic candidates for Kansas governor and US senator, including Governor Laura Kelly in both her campaigns, even though Kelly's 2022 Republican rival, then state Attorney General Derek Schmidt, had worked on Kassebaum Baker's Senate staff. In 2021, she also said President Donald Trump should be impeached after his supporters attacked the US Capitol in an attempt to stop Congress from certifying his 2020 defeat to Democrat Joe Biden. "This just has gone too far," she told Kansas City's KMBC.
Kassebaum Baker's career spanned elected office, bipartisan lawmaking and public service after retirement, and she remained closely identified with Kansas throughout. For many in the state and beyond, she was a centrist Republican who built a long Senate career while keeping a deliberately low-key style.

sources.news_title: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, former US senator from Kansas, dies at 94
sources.text:
Nancy Kassebaum Baker, former US senator from Kansas, dies at 94
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Nancy Kassebaum Baker, a Kansas governor’s daughter who became the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without following a spouse into office, has died. She was 94.
Kassebaum Baker died Friday of natural causes, according to her son, Bill Kassebaum.
“She loved Kansas. She loved people from Kansas and representing Kansas for 18 years in the U.S. Senate,” he told The Associated Press. “She was an independent-minded Republican who was willing to stand up for what she thought was right, even if that meant going against the party.”
She was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1978 and served three terms. Her modest demeanor endeared her to voters of all political stripes, though she shared the moderate, progressive Republican politics of her father, Gov. Alf Landon, the unsuccessful 1936 GOP nominee for president. Even after leaving the Senate early in 1997, she continued taking on public service roles.
She married former Sen. Howard Baker, a Tennessee Republican, in 1996. He died in 2014.
Kassebaum Baker remained an icon for Kansans generally. She could work with Senate colleagues of all political philosophies, and a 1996 health insurance law bore her name, along with that of liberal Massachusetts Sen. Ted Kennedy.
A centrist politician from America’s heartland
Her election to the Senate brought her immediate national attention. When she announced her retirement, she was among eight women senators and the only one to chair a Senate committee, the Labor and Human Resources panel.
She was also in a dwindling bloc of moderate-to-liberal Republicans, having supported for example a ban on assault weapons championed by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
Yet she never polarized Kansas conservatives as other GOP moderates did. She connected with voters because she never seemed caught up in the trappings of power, and when she retired, she acknowledged, “I’d rather cuddle up and do needlepoint all day.”
She was born on July 29, 1932, as her father, an oilman from Independence, was running for the first of his two terms as governor. She earned a political science degree from the University of Kansas and a master’s degree in diplomatic history from the University of Michigan in the mid-1950s.
She was a radio-station executive, spent a year in the 1970s on the staff of Kansas Sen. James Pearson and served on the school board in the Wichita suburb of Maize. She had four children with her first husband, Phil Kassebaum, including Bill, who served a term in the Kansas House. The marriage ended in divorce in 1979.
A moderate who sought sensible solutions
When Kassebaum Baker decided to run for the U.S. Senate, she figured that “a woman with a background different from a man might be appealing” to people growing weary of politics. Pundits at the time estimated a Senate race would require the then-huge-for-Kansas sum of $1 million. In the first quarter of 1978, she spent less than $12,000 on her campaign, and saw herself “at the bottom of the totem pole.”
However, nine candidates crowded the primary field, including three state senators and a prominent Wichita businessman. Kassebaum Baker won the GOP nomination with less than 31 percent of the vote.
Running as Nancy Landon Kassebaum, she won almost 54 percent of the vote that November against former two-term Democratic congressman Bill Roy.
Her moderate politics quickly came to the fore, when only months later, she refused to endorse an amendment to the U.S. Constitution to require a balanced budget.
“We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution,” she said.
Her father, who would die at age 100 in 1987, still cast a long political shadow during her first years in office. Though he’d overwhelmingly lost the 1936 presidential race to Democratic incumbent Franklin Roosevelt, he later became an elder statesman for the party. A lecture series named for him at Kansas State University attracted presidents and foreign leaders.
Kassebaum Baker became even more popular in her time. She won re-election in 1984 with 76 percent of the vote and in 1990 with 74 percent of the vote.
But she frustrated conservative activists, despite her popularity. She said her vote in favor of the assault weapons ban inspired the angriest mail of her career.
A public servant to the end
She’d contemplated not seeking a third term, but Republican leaders had prevailed upon her to run one more time. In 1996, when she decided not to seek re-election, she said she would return to a ranch and 90-year-old farmhouse in Kansas’ scenic Flint Hills and babysit her grandchildren — she had seven, as well as two great-grandchildren.
When there briefly was talk of naming a new highway in Topeka after her, she said, “Oh, goodness. Absolutely not — no.”
She and Baker kept their romance low-key, and speculation about a possible marriage didn’t emerge until mid-1996, in a Washington Post story. They married that December.
It was the first time a man and a woman who had both served in the Senate had wed. Baker was elected to three terms and served from 1967 to 1985 before becoming President Ronald Reagan’s chief of staff. His first wife, Joy, had died in 1993 after a long battle with cancer.
After the marriage, public service still beckoned, including as a member of a bipartisan commission on campaign finance reform under Clinton and on a British commission in Africa in 2004-05.
President George W. Bush named her husband ambassador to Japan in 2001, and she went with him for the four-year posting. Baker said she became an important figure in the Asian nation.
Before she left for Tokyo, she told a reporter she saw her stint in Japan as an adventure but added, “All I can say is, I will miss the Kansas prairie.”
Not a fan of Trump
Later in life, Kassebaum Baker broke with the Republican Party as it became more conservative, endorsing Democratic candidates for Kansas governor and U.S. senator, including Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly both times — even though Kelly’s 2022 GOP opponent, then state-Attorney General Derek Schmidt, had worked on her Senate staff.
She also declared in 2021 that President Donald Trump should be impeached after Trump supporters attacked the U.S. Capitol hoping to stop congressional certification of Trump’s defeat in 2020 by Democrat Joe Biden.
“This just has gone too far,” she told Kansas City’s KMBC.

sources.text:
Nancy Kassebaum, first woman to represent Kansas in U.S. Senate, dies at 94
FLINT HILLS, Kan. (KCTV) - Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker, the first woman to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate, has died at age 94, her granddaughter Nellie confirms.
Kassebaum’s family says she died Friday, Aug. 21. She was born July 29, 1932, in Topeka.
Kassebaum served in the U.S. Senate from 1978 to 1997. When she took office, she was the only woman in the U.S. Senate.
She was the daughter of Alf Landon, Kansas governor from 1933 to 1937 and the 1936 Republican nominee for president.
Her family says Kassebaum was sustained by the support of family and friends from around the globe, and that her life reflected remarkable success, real challenges, and above all, a deep love for Kansas.
A private memorial service will be held at a later date, her granddaughter adds.
In lieu of flowers, the family is asking the community to consider donations to the Kansas 4-H Foundation or the Capper Foundation.
“Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker, who hailed from a legendary political family, served Kansas herself with independence and decency for nearly two decades, then came home to the Flint Hills she loved,” Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson (R-Andover) says. “Kansas is grateful for her service. Marlo and I are praying for her family and all who loved her.”
“Saddened to hear of the passing of Senator Kassebaum,” adds U.S. Senator Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). “She was a true Kansan who dedicated years of her life to serving our state and made history as Kansas’ first woman to serve in the U.S. Senate. Laina and I are keeping her family and loved ones in our prayers.”
“Kansas awoke to sad news this morning,” notes U.S. Congressman Derek Schmidt (R-KS). “Senator Kassebaum introduced this kid from a small Southeast Kansas town to opportunities for public service I had not known possible. I worked for her five years and came away with cherished memories and friends who will last a lifetime. For her early mentorship, inspiration and example, I will always be deeply grateful.”
“We honor the life of Senator Nancy Kassebaum, a trailblazer who put the well-being of Kansans first. Her pioneering role as the first woman to represent our state in the U.S. Senate perfectly reflects the Kansas spirit. She was one of a kind, and she will be remembered among the greats who served the people of our state so well,” says U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). “Senator Kassebaum’s time in public service embodied the institution of the U.S. Senate at its best. I campaigned for her in western Kansas during her first election in 1978, as well as the campaigns that followed. She was never afraid to challenge me in our conversations, but she was always a friend and encourager. She was deeply respected across our state, and Kansans remain grateful for the way in which she represented us with such intelligence and integrity. Robba and I are keeping her children and the entire Kassebaum family in our thoughts as they mourn this loss. The legacy of the U.S. Senate, the well-being of our nation and, most significantly, the future of the state of Kansas are brighter because of the impact Senator Kassebaum had throughout her life. She will be deeply missed, but her legacy will never be forgotten.”
“Kansas lost part of its soul when Nancy Kassebaum died. Senator Kassebaum cared deeply about Kansas, about our country. No one worked harder, or smarter, to make our world a better place,” adds Governor Laura Kelly. “The first time I met her, 35 years ago, I knew I was in the presence of a unique human being. Humble, unassuming, while focused and fearless, Senator Kassebaum lived a life that mattered. I will miss her.”
Support and condolences continue to flood social media.

sources.news_title: Kansas political trailblazer Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker dies at 94
sources.text:
Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker, who fractured a political glass ceiling as the first woman to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate, died Friday.
Kassebaum, 94, grew up in Topeka and began her personal journey in politics as a member of the Maize school board. In 1978, she defeated eight Republicans to seize the nomination for U.S. Senate in a contest to determine who took the seat held by retiring Republican U.S. Sen. James Pearson. She prevailed in that general election with 53% of the vote but easily won reelection contests in 1984 and 1990 with more than 70% of the vote.
The Kassebaum family confirmed her death in a statement reported by KSNT that noted her remarkable life and appreciation for Kansas.
“For 94 years she relished the support of family and friends from all over the world. Her years were filled with remarkable successes, challenges and above all a deep love for Kansas,” the statement said.
The family intends to conduct a private memorial service at an unspecified date. Memorial donations are to be directed to the Capper Foundation and the Kansas 4-H Foundation, the statement said.
Kassebaum, the widow of retired U.S. Sen. Howard Baker of Tennessee and the daughter of 1936 presidential nominee and Gov. Alf Landon, had the distinction of being the second woman elected to the U.S. Senate without her spouse having previously served as a member of Congress.
Kassebaum was known for her political independence, moderate sensibilities and advocacy of bipartisanship on domestic and international affairs during her 18 years in Washington, D.C.
She supported the Equal Rights Amendment, abortion rights, a ban on assault weapons and the end of apartheid in South Africa. She was among Senate champions of creating a federal holiday to honor the late Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. After leaving elective politics, she voiced objections to GOP President Donald Trump and endorsed Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.
In 2022, she said during a program at the Dole Institute of Politics at the University of Kansas that it would have been impossible for her to win elective office in the modern era.
“I know full well I could not be reelected today,” she said. “It’s not that I’ve changed so much.”
In the Landon home, her father had been skeptical of her underdog campaign to win a cherished seat in the U.S. Senate. He understood defeat after getting crushed by President Franklin Roosevelt in 1936.
“I talked to the family about it, who all sort of rolled their eyes. My father did not want me to run. I think he thought I would lose,” Kassebaum said.
She decided to run and took note of her father’s reputation among Kansans with the campaign slogan: “A Fresh Face: A Trusted Kansas Name.”
Kassebaum said U.S. Sen. Robert Dole of Kansas, who died in 2021, assisted her campaign by convincing Republicans that she would be a capable senator for Kansas. In 2015, Dole told the Wichita Eagle that Kassebaum had been one of the most popular politicians in the state.
“Nancy has a way about her that she gets along with everyone. She has never tried to be a moderate or a conservative,” Dole said.
Kassebaum was born July 29, 1932, and grew up in Topeka. She earned a bachelor’s degree at the University of Kansas and a master’s degree in diplomatic history at the University of Michigan.
She married her first husband, John Philip Kassebaum, and they had four children — John, Linda, Richard and William. The Kassebaum’s divorced in 1979.
After deciding not to seek a fourth term but still a member of the U.S. Senate, she married Baker in 1996. The Rev. John Danforth, the former senator from Missouri, performed the ceremony. President George W. Bush appointed Baker to serve as ambassador to Japan. Baker and Kassebaum lived in Japan for four years. Baker died in 2014. She resided on a ranch in Morris County.
This story was originally published in the Kansas Reflector.

sources.news_title: Pioneering former US Senator Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker dies
sources.text:
Former U.S. Senator Nancy Landon Kassebaum Baker, a moderate Republican who became the first woman elected to the Senate from Kansas, has died aged 94, according to local reports.
Kassebaum Baker died Friday in Topeka, Kansas. She was born in Topeka in 1932 and entered the Senate in 1978, serving until her retirement in 1997.
The daughter of former Kansas governor and 1936 Republican presidential candidate Alf Landon, Kassebaum Baker became a prominent moderate voice in the Republican Party and was known for working across party lines during her three terms in the Senate.
Newsweek contacted Kansas state representatives via email Saturday for comment.
"Born on July 29, 1932, in Topeka, Kansas, for 94 years she relished the support of family and friends from all over the world. Her years were filled with remarkable successes, challenges, and above all, a deep love for Kansas," her family said in a statement, as reported by KSNT.
The family said a private memorial service will be held at a later date and asked for donations to be made to the Kansas 4-H Foundation or the Capper Foundation, as per the outlet.
From Kansas Politics To The US Senate
Kassebaum Baker graduated from the University of Kansas in 1954 and earned a master's degree in history from the University of Michigan in 1956. That same year, she married her first husband, Philip Kassebaum, and later became vice president of Kassebaum Communications, as per AWPC (Archives of Women's Political Communication).
Before entering the Senate, she worked in the family communications business, served on a local school board and worked in Senator James B. Pearson's office.
The Topeka native was elected to the Senate in 1978 after winning a closely contested Republican primary and general election. She was re-elected in 1984 and 1990, serving Kansas for 18 years. She was the first female senator ever elected to a full term without a husband who served in Congress.
By the time she retired in 1997, nine women were serving as senators.
In 1995, she became chairwoman of the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, making her the first woman to chair a major standing Senate committee. She also played a leading role in health-based legislation, working with Democratic Senator Edward Kennedy on the 1996 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, commonly known as the Kassebaum-Kennedy Act.
The law expanded protections for people changing jobs and dealing with pre-existing medical conditions.
A Bipartisan Voice In Washington
A moderate Republican known for her independent approach, she also worked on issues including deficit reduction, ending apartheid in South Africa, and reforms to general aviation liability laws.
Her bipartisan approach sometimes put Kassebaum Baker at odds with members of her own party. She supported legislation on health care, education and labor issues and was also involved in efforts to reduce the federal budget deficit and address arms control.
Just before leaving the Senate in 1997, Kassebaum Baker married former Tennessee senator and Senate majority leader Howard Baker. He later served as US ambassador to Japan. She subsequently divided her time between Kansas and Tennessee.
Kassebaum Baker's Legacy
The former senator discussed her life and career in a 2017 interview for the Senate’s Women of the Senate Oral History Project.
When asked by the interviewer about her first major legislative effort in her political career, she recalled becoming closely involved with the Foreign Relations Committee, particularly on arms control and conflicts in Central America. She led a U.S. delegation observing El Salvador’s elections, where she remembered hearing “gunfire still in the streets.”
Asked if she saw herself as a role model, she said: “I’m happy if people think that. I don’t ever want to discourage anyone and would encourage. I believe it’s important to do. And I go back to being able to study history, study politics….we all can learn. I can learn a lot."
Regarding her decision to retire, she said after 18 years in the Senate, she “wanted to come back home" and therefore announced in 1995 that she would not seek a fourth term.
Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.
